problem: Existing MLLMs and VLN benchmarks generate instructions for static, simple settings and never decide whether or when to speak. This leads to verbose, badly timed, or unsafe guidance for blind pedestrians, for example talking while the user crosses an intersection.
motivation: Poorly timed or wrong instructions (left vs right, chatter at crossings) can be dangerous and add cognitive load for blind users. Mobility guides stress concise cues, silence at intersections, and warnings about obstacles within cane length, and no video-based benchmark captures this.
key_idea: Build TIMELI, a large CARLA-based video benchmark for time-aware assistive navigation instruction generation, and improve MLLMs by supervising a predicted reason before each instruction plus an auxiliary binary timing head that decides whether to speak.
insight: Off-the-shelf MLLMs (Timing F1 around 0.5 or below, low BLEU-4) fail at when-to-speak, and fine-tuning alone is insufficient. Adding history, plan and reason supervision (LLaVA-v1.6 to LLaVA-v1.6+) raises Timing F1 from 0.572 to 0.776, and the timing head (++) adds a little more (0.792). Image-based models beat video-based ones, which the authors attribute to weak long-context video compression. Open-loop language metrics do not always predict closed-loop success.
method: Task formulation: at each step the model gets an egocentric video/frame, a task spec, a text command plus 2D waypoint from a coarse map planner, and timestamped instruction history. It outputs an instruction or 'None' to stay silent.

TIMELI-Sim data: CARLA pedestrian simulation with 67K videos at 1 FPS (RGB, depth, segmentation, location) across 5 towns and 6 weather conditions. Procedural instructions cover directional cues, obstacle alerts (repeat suppression, except within 1 m), and junction enter/exit warnings, and 79.1% of steps are silent.

TIMELI-Real: 2,000 YouTube videos, annotated with a GPT-4o-suggested-text interface and mobility-guide rules, used only for validation. Design was informed by a pilot study with 10 blind participants and O&M guides.

Reason prediction: the output is restructured to first predict one of 8 reason labels (remain silent, silent in junction, enter/exit junction, obstacle in front, constant instruction, direction change, stop), then the instruction.

Timing supervision: a binary head takes an MLP encoding of the past-instruction trace vector plus visual features and predicts whether to issue an instruction. It can gate inference with an early exit. Loss = CE(reason) + CE(instruction) + beta*BCE(issue).

Evaluation: open-loop BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, Timing F1/AUC (1 s tolerance) and conciseness. Closed-loop CARLA on 12 routes with noisy goal (2 m) and heading (5°), reporting SR, route completion, navigation score, collisions/min, instructions/min and a composite NQS.

setting.backbone: LLaVA-v1.6-7B (fine-tuned, main); also TinyLLaVA-3B, VILA-3B video, TimeChat-7B fine-tuned; GPT-4o etc. as off-the-shelf baselines
setting.training_data: TIMELI-Sim synthetic CARLA videos (training on Town05 and Town10; the 67K-video total is over all towns) with procedurally generated instructions and reason labels; no real data
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (frame or video) plus noisy relative goal coordinates, high-level plan command and instruction history
setting.action_space: text instruction generation (or None), mapped to pedestrian movement via a rule-based function in closed loop
setting.privileged: none at test time (noisy GPS and a coarse planner are assumed inputs); reason labels come from simulator state only for training supervision

numbers_note: SR in closed-loop is printed as a fraction (0.50), not a percentage. Benchmark names are custom, and there is no canonical benchmark. Timing metrics are fractions as printed. The paper's own text says the LLaVA-v1.6++ model reaches an SR 'up to 50%'.
results: Off-the-shelf models perform poorly (best GPT-4o image BLEU-4 7.395, Timing F1 0.451), while fine-tuned LLaVA-v1.6+/++ reach Timing F1 0.776/0.792. In closed loop LLaVA-v1.6++ achieves NQS 0.82 and 50% SR versus 0.31 NQS and 4% SR for the un-augmented fine-tuned LLaVA-v1.6. Sim-to-real transfer works for image models (Timing F1 0.672–0.732) but degrades for video models.
limitations: Closed-loop evaluation uses a rule-based instruction-to-action mapping rather than real blind users, on only 12 simulated routes; real-world data is used only for open-loop validation.

Persistent weaknesses in temporal reasoning, safety-critical object awareness and distance/relational understanding; video models underperform image models, and conciseness drops with the timing head.
Trained only on synthetic CARLA data, with some real-world degradation and no real-robot or user deployment.
